Ice_Plant___healthy.name: Ice Plant (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Ice_Plant___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Ice Plant.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Idaho_Potato___healthy.name: Idaho Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Idaho_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Idaho Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Japanese_Sweet_Potato___healthy.name: Japanese Sweet Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Japanese_Sweet_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Japanese Sweet Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Jicama.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Kabocha_Squash___healthy.name: Kabocha Squash (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Kabocha_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Kabocha Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.

Leek___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Leek.

Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.

New_Potato___healthy.name: New Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
New_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime New Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Okinawan_Sweet_Potato___healthy.name: Okinawan Sweet Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Okinawan_Sweet_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Okinawan Sweet Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

disease_symptoms.s1: Plump, firm globe-shaped bulbs with crisp, dry, paper-like golden or red outer wrapper scales.
disease_symptoms.s2: Tubular, hollow blue-green cylindrical leaves standing upright with zero purple blotch or thrips stippling.
disease_symptoms.s3: Tight, well-sealed neck tissue indicating proper maturity and excellent storage potential.

disease_causes.c1: Correct photoperiod (short-day or long-day according to latitude) in loose, rich, friable soil.

disease_prevention.p1: Avoid deep planting; onion bulbs should form right at the soil surface.
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure wide row spacing (25-30 cm) and avoid overhead irrigation to prevent foliar blight.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced organic base fertilizer (NPK 5-10-10) with sulfur (gypsum or sulfate of potash) for pungency.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Side-dress with calcium nitrate at early leaf expansion; stop feeding once bulbing initiates.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: No chemical intervention needed for prime healthy onion bulbs.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Spinosad or blue sticky cards if onion thrips pressure rises.

organic_remedies.org1: Dust diatomaceous earth around row margins to deter onion maggots.
organic_remedies.org2: Mulch between rows with straw to prevent weed competition without burying bulb necks.

disease_control.ctrl1: When 50-70% of tops naturally fall over, bend remaining tops; cure bulbs in warm dry shade.

Pattypan_Squash___healthy.name: Pattypan Squash (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Pattypan_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Pattypan Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

Pear_Squash___healthy.name: Pear Squash (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Pear_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Pear Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

Perilla___healthy.name: Perilla (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Perilla___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Perilla.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Peruvian_Purple_Potato___healthy.name: Peruvian Purple Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Peruvian_Purple_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Peruvian Purple Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Pignut___healthy.name: Pignut (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Pignut___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Pignut.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Prairie_Turnip___healthy.name: Prairie Turnip (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Prairie_Turnip___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Prairie Turnip.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Pumpkin_Kaddu___healthy.name: Pumpkin / Kaddu (Cucurbita moschata)
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Pumpkin / Kaddu.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

sources: All Vegetables (NZ Māori & Global Botanical Index)
Koppert India & ICAR Plant Protection Standards

Purple_Carrot___healthy.name: Purple Carrot (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Purple_Carrot___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Purple Carrot.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.

organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.

pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.

Red_Bliss_Potato___healthy.name: Red Bliss Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Red_Bliss_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Red Bliss Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.

symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Red Warty Thing Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.

Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.

Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

Red_Wing_Onion___healthy.name: Red Wing Onion (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Red_Wing_Onion___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Red Wing Onion.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.
Implement 4-year crop rotation excluding other allium crops.
fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.
Spinetoram or Spinosad for thrips suppression under heavy pressure.

symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Soko.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.

Spaghetti_Squash___healthy.name: Spaghetti Squash (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Spaghetti_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Spaghetti Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Stokes Purple Sweet Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Striped_Eggplant___healthy.name: Striped Eggplant (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Striped_Eggplant___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia

Specimen shows strong cellular defense with zero necrotic spots or pathogen lesions.
causes: Favorable climate with balanced sunlight, temperature, and moisture conditions.
Fertile, well-aerated soil structure with appropriate nutrient availability.
Adequate agronomic care following integrated pest and nutrient management principles.
prevention: Select certified disease-resistant crop cultivars and clean planting material.
Maintain clean cultivation, weed eradication, and field sanitation.
Monitor crop fields twice weekly for early detection of pests or physiological stress.
fertilizer: Soil-test-based balanced NPK application supplemented with well-rotted organic manure.

organic: Koppert biological control solutions tailored to pest and pathogen pressure.
Trichoderma and Pseudomonas bio-inoculants for root zone health and systemic acquired resistance.
Botanical neem oil formulations (1500 - 10000 ppm) for preventive insect control.
pesticides: Integrate biorational biopesticides and target-specific registered crop protection agents.
Observe proper pre-harvest intervals (PHI) and rotation of chemical modes of action.

Summer_Cilantro___healthy.name: Summer Cilantro (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Summer_Cilantro___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Summer Cilantro.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Summer_Squash___healthy.name: Summer Squash (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Summer_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Summer Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

Sweet_Onion___healthy.name: Sweet Onion (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Sweet_Onion___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Sweet Onion.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.
Implement 4-year crop rotation excluding other allium crops.
fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.
Spinetoram or Spinosad for thrips suppression under heavy pressure.

Sweet_Potato_Leaves___healthy.name: Sweet Potato Leaves (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Sweet_Potato_Leaves___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Sweet Potato Leaves.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Taro_Leaves___healthy.name: Taro Leaves (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Taro_Leaves___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Taro Leaves.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.

organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.

Tuberous_Nasturtium___healthy.name: Tuberous Nasturtium (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Tuberous_Nasturtium___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Tuberous Nasturtium.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

sources: All Vegetables (NZ Māori & Global Botanical Index)
Koppert India & ICAR Plant Protection Standards

Tuscan_Kale___healthy.name: Tuscan Kale (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Tuscan_Kale___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Tuscan Kale.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Udupi_Mattu_Gulla_Eggplant___healthy.condition: Healthy Udupi Mattu Gulla Eggplant Specimen
Udupi_Mattu_Gulla_Eggplant___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vegetative growth and species-typical morphology for prime Udupi Mattu Gulla Eggplant.
Healthy foliar color, robust stems, and optimal reproductive flowering/fruiting vigor.
Specimen shows strong cellular defense with zero necrotic spots or pathogen lesions.
causes: Favorable climate with balanced sunlight, temperature, and moisture conditions.
Fertile, well-aerated soil structure with appropriate nutrient availability.
Adequate agronomic care following integrated pest and nutrient management principles.
prevention: Select certified disease-resistant crop cultivars and clean planting material.
Maintain clean cultivation, weed eradication, and field sanitation.
Monitor crop fields twice weekly for early detection of pests or physiological stress.
fertilizer: Soil-test-based balanced NPK application supplemented with well-rotted organic manure.
Balanced micronutrient cocktail (Zinc, Iron, Manganese, Boron) via foliar application.
Humic and fulvic acid soil drenches to optimize root nutrient absorption capacity.
organic: Koppert biological control solutions tailored to pest and pathogen pressure.
Trichoderma and Pseudomonas bio-inoculants for root zone health and systemic acquired resistance.
Botanical neem oil formulations (1500 - 10000 ppm) for preventive insect control.
pesticides: Integrate biorational biopesticides and target-specific registered crop protection agents.
Observe proper pre-harvest intervals (PHI) and rotation of chemical modes of action.

Umbrella_Squash___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Umbrella Squash.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Vidalia Onions.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.

fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.

Vitelotte_Potato___healthy.name: Vitelotte Potato (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Vitelotte_Potato___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Vitelotte Potato.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Walking_Onion___healthy.name: Walking Onion (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Walking_Onion___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Walking Onion.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.
Implement 4-year crop rotation excluding other allium crops.
fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.
Spinetoram or Spinosad for thrips suppression under heavy pressure.

Wasabi___healthy.name: Wasabi (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Wasabi___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Wasabi.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Watercress___healthy.name: Watercress (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Watercress___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Watercress.
Uniform green lamina with clear epidermal venation and zero signs of chlorotic spotting or downy mildew sporulation.
Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.
Spinosad biorational formulation for caterpillar and leaf miner management.

Wax_Gourd___healthy.name: Wax Gourd (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Wax_Gourd___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Wax Gourd.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.

Welsh_Onion___healthy.name: Welsh Onion (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Welsh_Onion___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in Welsh Onion.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.
Implement 4-year crop rotation excluding other allium crops.
fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.
Spinetoram or Spinosad for thrips suppression under heavy pressure.

White_Onion___healthy.name: White Onion (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
White_Onion___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Erect, tubular cylindrical foliage with healthy blue-green waxy cuticular bloom in White Onion.
Firm bulb development with tight, dry outer scales and well-anchored root system.
Zero lesions, purple blotch, tip dieback, or basal plate rot.
causes: Sufficient photoperiod (short-day or long-day) triggering bulb swelling.
Cool early vegetative phase (13-24°C) followed by warmer ripening conditions (25-35°C).
Loose, fertile soil with pH 6.0-7.0 and excellent drainage.
prevention: Avoid deep transplanting; set seedlings or cloves at recommended 2-3 cm depth.
Withhold irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to allow neck closure and scale curing.
Implement 4-year crop rotation excluding other allium crops.
fertilizer: NPK 8-15-15 basal application with sulfur (30 kg/ha elemental S) to enhance pungency and bulb quality.
Top-dress with urea or ammonium sulfate before bulb initiation; cease N at bulking.
Zinc sulfate (2 g/L) spray at 30 and 45 days after planting.
organic: Koppert Thripex (Neoseiulus cucumeris) for predatory control of onion thrips (Thrips tabaci).
Pseudomonas fluorescens seed and bulb treatment against damping off and basal rot.
Verticillium lecanii (Lecanicillium) bio-insecticide for thrips nymph control.
pesticides: Mancozeb (2.5 g/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L) for purple blotch and Stemphylium blight control.
Spinetoram or Spinosad for thrips suppression under heavy pressure.

symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Witch Hazel.

Petiole and stem tissues demonstrate high cell turgor and resilience against foliar lodging.
causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.
Balanced soil pH of 6.2 - 7.0 with well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam.
Good air circulation between plant canopies minimizing relative humidity buildup.
prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.
Ensure plant spacing of 20-30 cm to allow sunlight penetration and canopy ventilation.
fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.
Foliar spray of Seaweed extract (2 ml/L) for micronutrient supplementation (Iron, Magnesium, Manganese).
Calcium nitrate (1 g/L) side-dressing during vegetative expansion to prevent tip-burn.
organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.
Bacillus subtilis biological preventive spray against downy mildew and leaf blight.
Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.

Yam___healthy.name: Yam (Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia)
Yam___healthy.pathogen: Botanical classification per GoodGoodGood Vegetable Encyclopedia
symptoms: Robust root development, uniform taper, and healthy dermal skin typical of prime Yam.
Foliar crown shows vigorous vegetative petiole growth without stunting, yellowing, or leaf curl.
Subterranean storage tissue free from nematode galling, wireworm tunnels, or bacterial soft rot.
causes: Deep, loose, stone-free friable soil allowing unrestricted taproot and tuber expansion.
Optimum soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8 with adequate potassium reserves.
Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.
Long crop rotation cycle with alliums and cereals to break root-knot nematode cycles.
Solarization of nursery beds and certified disease-free seed tubers or certified seed stock.
fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.
Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum) for suppression of Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium rots.
Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

Consistent moisture regime preventing root cracking, splitting, or hollow heart.
prevention: Deep plowing (30 cm) and ridge or raised bed planting to enhance drainage and aeration.

fertilizer: NPK 5-10-15 or 6-12-18 emphasizing potassium and phosphorus for storage organ enlargement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen which causes excessive top growth and split, hairy roots.
Boron (Solubor 1 g/L) application at root bulking to prevent internal black heart or browning.
organic: Koppert Larvanem (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) against root grubs, wireworms, and root maggots.

Trichoderma viride bio-fertilizer enriched in vermicompost applied at sowing/planting.
pesticides: Biorational Bacillus thuringiensis for cutworms and soil application of Metarhizium anisopliae.
Fluopyram or bio-nematicides for root-knot nematode suppression.

symptoms: Vibrant, turgid foliage with optimal chlorophyll density characteristic of healthy Yerba Buena.

causes: Optimum temperature range between 15°C and 22°C with adequate cool root-zone moisture.

prevention: Maintain morning drip irrigation to ensure foliage dries thoroughly before nightfall.
Implement 3-year crop rotation with non-chenopod and non-brassica crops.

fertilizer: NPK 10-10-10 or 8-4-8 balanced baseline fertilizer supplemented with compost tea.

organic: Koppert Trianum-P (Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22) for root shield and soil-borne protection.

Neem oil (Azadirachtin 0.03% EC at 3 ml/L) against aphids, thrips, and leaf miners.
pesticides: Potassium silicate or Copper oxychloride (2 g/L) as a protective botanical fungicide if humidity exceeds 85%.

Bottle_Gourd_Lauki___healthy.name: Bottle Gourd / Lauki (Lagenaria siceraria)
symptoms: Vigorous vine elongation, healthy palmate foliage, and prolific flowering in Bottle Gourd / Lauki.
Uniform fruit set without blossom-end decay, fruit fly oviposition marks, or mosaic mottling.
Deep green leaves with zero powdery mildew superficial white powder on adaxial surfaces.
causes: Warm growing season with temperatures between 24°C and 32°C and high solar irradiance.
Well-drained sandy loam soil enriched with matured farmyard manure (FYM).
Optimal pollination assisted by beneficial honeybees and bumblebees.
prevention: Trellising and vertical staking systems to keep vines and fruit elevated above wet soil.
Pheromone cue-lure traps (10-12 traps/acre) for fruit fly (Bactrocera cucurbitae) suppression.
Drip irrigation to avoid wetting foliage and prevent powdery and downy mildew outbreaks.
fertilizer: NPK 10-26-26 or 12-32-16 at basal stage followed by soluble potassium nitrate during fruit sizing.
Calcium chelate foliar spray during flowering to avert blossom-end rot.
Magnesium sulfate (5 g/L) to maintain vigorous photosynthesis in large vine canopies.
organic: Koppert Swirski-Mite (Amblyseius swirskii) against thrips, whiteflies, and spider mites.
Koppert Spical (Neoseiulus californicus) for biological spider mite management.
Ampelomyces quisqualis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide against powdery mildew.
pesticides: Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) spray against early sap-sucking pests.
Sulfur-based wettable fungicide (2 g/L) or Copper hydroxide for foliar disease management.
